summary:
Describe a word by its **shape**: replace each letter by the order in which that letter first appeared
(`"boot"` → 0, 1, 1, 2). Two words have the same shape exactly when these sequences are equal. Compute
the pattern's shape once and compare every word's shape to it, O(total letters).

question.md:
Count the words that can be turned into `pattern` by a **consistent, one-to-one** letter replacement.

- **Consistent:** a letter always becomes the same letter. In `"moon"` → `"feet"`, both o's become e.
- **One-to-one:** different letters must become different letters. `"moan"` can't become `"feet"`
  (o and a would both have to become e), and `"cc"` can't become `"xy"` (one c can't become two
  letters).
- **Lengths must match.** Different lengths can never have the same shape.
- **Single letters all match:** any one-letter word has the shape of any other.
- **Size:** up to 10⁴ words, each at most 20 letters.

think.md:
Take pattern `"boot"` and the words feet, moon, moan, deed, abba, keep.

Ignore what the letters *are* and look at where they **repeat**. In `boot` the middle two letters are
the same and everything else is different. Write that down by numbering letters in order of first
appearance: b is new (0), o is new (1), o again (1), t is new (2): **0 1 1 2**.

think.caption: feet, moon and keep have the pattern's shape 0 1 1 2.

think.md:
This numbering captures exactly the two rules: a repeated letter repeats its number (consistent), and
a new letter always gets a new number (one-to-one). So "same shape" becomes "same number sequence",
a plain equality check, and the sequence works as a **group key** too.

approaches.title: Check every pair of positions

idea.md: Two strings of equal length have the same shape exactly when, for every pair of positions `i < j`, the word's letters are equal if and only if the pattern's letters are equal. Check all pairs.

build: For each word of the right length, loop over all position pairs `i < j`.
If `(w[i] == w[j]) != (p[i] == p[j])`, the shapes differ.
Count the words with no disagreement.

lines.text: Check each word against the pattern.
A different length can't have the same shape.
Equal letters in the word must sit exactly where the pattern has equal letters, for every pair of positions. That single rule covers both "consistent" and "one-to-one".

complexity.md: **Time O(N · L²)** for N words of length L: L(L − 1)/2 pairs per word. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: Pattern 'boot': positions 1 and 2 are equal, every other pair differs.
'moon': all 6 position pairs agree with the pattern. Same shape.
'moan': positions 1 and 2 are different in the word but equal in the pattern. Not the same shape.
'deed': positions 0 and 3 are equal in the word but different in the pattern. Not the same shape.
Checking all six words this way: 3 match (feet, moon, keep).

walk.title: For every pair of positions, letters must be equal in the word exactly when they're equal in the pattern.

limits.md: Each pair is compared from scratch. Remembering what each letter maps to as you scan replaces the pairs with a single pass.

approaches.title: Two-way letter mapping

idea.md:
Scan the word and pattern together, building two maps: word letter → pattern letter, and pattern
letter → word letter. A word letter that's already mapped to something else breaks consistency; a
pattern letter that already stands for a different word letter breaks one-to-one. If neither
happens, the shapes match. With 26 letters, both maps are arrays of 26.

build: Skip words of a different length.
At each position with letters x (word) and y (pattern): if `fwd[x]` is set and isn't y, or `back[y]` is set and isn't x, fail. Otherwise set both.
Count the words that never fail.

lines.text: Only words of the pattern's length can match.
`fwd` maps word letters to pattern letters; `back` maps the other way. Both start empty (0 means unmapped).

notes.python: Plain dictionaries; with 26 letters an array would work too.

lines.text: Walk the word and the pattern side by side.
Neither letter has a partner yet: pair them up in both directions.

Otherwise both must already be paired **with each other**. A mismatch in `fwd` breaks consistency (one word letter would need two different pattern letters). A mismatch in `back` breaks one-to-one: in `"moan"` against `"boot"`, o and a would both have to become o, and only the reverse map notices.

notes.python: `setdefault` returns the existing value or stores the new one, so one comparison per direction does both the check and the insert.

lines.text: Count words with a consistent two-way mapping.

complexity.md: **Time O(N · L):** one pass per word. **Space O(1):** two 26-letter maps.

steps.text: 'moon': mappings m→b, o→o, n→t stay consistent both ways. Same shape.
'moan' position 2: pattern letter 'o' already stands for 'o', now it would be 'a'. Conflict.
'deed' position 3: 'd' was already mapped to 'b', now it would need 't'. Conflict.
Count of words passing the check: 3.

walk.title: Build the letter mapping word → pattern and pattern → word as you go; any conflict means a different shape.

limits.md: Correct and linear, but it needs two maps, and forgetting the reverse map is the classic bug. It also only answers "does this word match that pattern?"; it doesn't give each word a key you could group or hash by.

approaches.title: Compare canonical shapes

idea.md:
Map each string to its shape: walk it and replace each letter by the order of its first appearance
(0 for the first new letter, 1 for the second, …). Compute the pattern's shape once, then count the
words whose shape is equal. One map per string, no reverse map needed: two different letters can
never receive the same number, so one-to-one is built in.

build: Write `shape(s)`: a 26-slot table of first-appearance numbers, filled as letters are first seen.
Count the words with `shape(word) == target` (different lengths give different shapes).

lines.text: The canonical shape: each letter is replaced by the order of its first appearance. A letter seen before reuses its number; a new letter takes the next number.

notes.python: `first.setdefault(ch, len(first))` returns the letter's existing number, or gives it the next one (the current size of the map).
notes.c: Words are at most 20 letters, so a fixed buffer of 21 ints holds any shape.

lines.text: A word matches exactly when its shape equals the pattern's. Different lengths give different-length shapes, so they never compare equal.

notes.c: Compare lengths first, then the numbers with `memcmp`.

complexity.md: **Time O(N · L):** each string's shape takes one pass. **Space O(L)** for the shape being compared.

steps.text: Pattern 'boot' → [0, 1, 1, 2]: b is the 0th new letter, o the 1st, t the 2nd.

walk.title: Replace each letter by the order in which it first appeared. Words with the same shape get the same numbers.

takeaways.md:
- "Equal up to renaming" problems (isomorphic strings, word patterns) become simple equality once you
  map each item to a **canonical form**: number things in order of first appearance.
- A canonical form is also a **group key**: you could count how many words share each shape with a
  hash map.
- If you check a mapping directly instead, check **both directions**; one map alone lets two letters
  collapse into one.
